column2: Decisions and mechanisms of intergroup bias in children's third-party punishment
column8: In the first phase, participants were shown two colored caps and asked to choose the team they wanted to be part of (orange or green). Then, subjects were asked to wear the team-colored cap they chose based on their preference (see Figure 1, left panel). By this procedure, children were assigned to their own group (ingroup), and their outgroup was defined.
column18: Afterwards, participants were told that pairs of children from the classroom/center had recently played a game in which one of the players, the actor, decided how to distribute six pieces of candy between himself/herself and the other player, the recipient. Actors and recipients were represented with emoji faces, identical to those used in the previous phase, and were pasted in two transparent empty candy jars (see Figure 1, right panel). The experimenter explained that neither of these players will receive the pieces of candy until he/she (the participant) decides whether to accept or reject each allocation offer. If the participant accepts the offer, each player will receive the pieces of candy and the participant will fill each player?????s jar with the corresponding candy. If the participant rejects the offer, neither player will receive candy. Thus, if participants would only reject selfish offers, the rejection of such offer means a punishment to the actor/transgressor (i.e., he/she will not receive the six pieces of candy of this trial).

column8: To magnify potential contrasts in group identity, we adopted a realworld group manipulation in which participants chose their team according to their preference for either cats or dogs instead of using the minimal group paradigm. Participants were asked to choose a cat team or a dog team, and then they were randomly assigned to the low or high group identity conditions. In the manipulated low identity condition, participants (n = 68) were informed that the team of their choice was full, and thus they were automatically assigned to the other team. By contrast, in the manipulated high identity condition, participants (n = 66) were told that they successfully joined the team they had chosen. We assumed that participants who voluntarily joined the team might become more strongly identified members compared with their counterparts who were assigned to the team.
